worksheet.title: The Wrong Direction
worksheet.subtitle: A move goes the wrong way — fix it
worksheet.learning_goal: I can find a move that goes the wrong way and fix its direction.

parts.title: The goal: both reach 2
parts.text: Bit (green) and Pixel (purple) both start on the green flag. They should BOTH reach number 2. One script is correct, but the other has a move going the WRONG WAY — forward when it should go back. Read both, find the wrong direction, and fix it.

parts.title: Run both
parts.prompt: Where does each land? Bit (home 0, forward 2): ____  Pixel (home 4, forward 2): ____. (Remember: a sprite cannot go past 5.) Which one misses the goal 2?

parts.title: Find the wrong direction
parts.prompt: Pixel starts at 4 and needs to reach 2. Is 2 in FRONT of Pixel or BEHIND it? So which way should Pixel move — forward or back?

parts.title: Fix it
parts.prompt: Write Pixel's fixed move: ____ 2 (forward or back?). After the fix, where does Pixel land? Do both reach the goal now?

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: A move can have the right number but the wrong DIRECTION. Look at where the sprite starts and where the goal is: if the goal is behind it, the move must go back, not forward. Here Pixel needed back 2, not forward 2.

teacher_guide.eyebrow: Teacher Guide · Grade 2 · Debugging & Reading Code
teacher_guide.title: The Wrong Direction
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students fix a wrong-DIRECTION bug in one of two parallel scripts (C3.2 alter + C3.1 write). The goal is 'both reach 2'; Bit is correct, but Pixel moves forward (away from 2, overshooting to 5) when it should move back. Students reason about where the goal is relative to the sprite's home and change the direction. This builds direction sense alongside debugging.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum (Grade 2 — C3 Coding)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: The printed worksheet and a pencil. Optional: a star on square 2; place a counter on Pixel's home (4) and ask 'is the star in front or behind?' before choosing the direction.

parts.title: Run it (about 20 min)
text: 1. I DO: state the goal — 'both reach 2.' Run Bit: 0 forward 2 → 2 (correct).
2. WE DO: run Pixel: 4 forward 2 → tries 6 but stops at 5 (the path ends at 5). 'Pixel went the wrong way — away from 2.'
3. YOU DO: students see the goal 2 is BEHIND Pixel (which is at 4), so the move should be back 2; they fix it and confirm Pixel reaches 2.
4. Connect: 'Check the direction: if the goal is behind the sprite, the move must go back.'

parts.title: Answer key (modelled by the run-gate)
text: Ex 1 — Bit: 0 → forward 2 → 2 (reaches goal). Pixel: 4 → forward 2 → 5 (the path stops at 5; Pixel overshoots and misses 2).
Ex 2 — the goal 2 is BEHIND Pixel (Pixel is at 4), so Pixel should move BACK, not forward.
Ex 3 — fixed move: back 2 → Pixel lands on 2. Now BOTH reach the goal 2.
Fix note: the number (2) was fine; only the direction changes from forward to back.

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common error: changing the number instead of the direction — here the count of 2 is correct; the direction is the bug.
Common error: forgetting the path stops at 5 — forward from 4 cannot reach 6, so Pixel sits at 5.
Simplify: ask 'is the star in front of Pixel or behind it?' to choose the direction.
Extend: ask which direction Bit would need if Bit started at 4 like Pixel (back 2 as well).
Success indicator: the child changes Pixel's move to back 2 and confirms both reach 2.
